name: Karl Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the fourth Bauer to milk cows at Lindenhof. It's 90 hectares, 80 dairy cows, grass for silage and some barley. I'm in the parlour at five, then feeding, then whatever the day throws at you, then milking again at four. Eight years ago I took out a mortgage to buy my sister out of her share, and I don't regret it. It's hard, but it's ours.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Inspectors and forms, more than the cows. Every year there's a new rule written by someone who's never seen a calf born. My wife Greta works mornings in the school kitchen, and we've got Johann, who's fifteen, and Lotte, who's eleven. I don't use any of that AI. Johann tried to show me once, and I told him to go and wash the parlour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's the one I'd vote for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said all along: it's mostly salesmen and city talk. Farming is work, and work doesn't come out of a computer. I'd say that after church and at the dairy farmers' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays as it is, and I'm glad. My worries are the milk price, the bank and the rules, same as my father's were. AI was never going to milk my cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. We'd keep paying the mortgage and putting a bit by, maybe 120 a month. I might finally replace the old bulk milk tank, which is about 15,000, but only if the milk price holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Satisfied, if I'm honest, that I didn't fall for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone who'd be disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Johann, probably. He's always on his phone looking at robot milkers and asking why we don't have one. I'd tell him a robot doesn't know when a cow's got mastitis just by the way she stands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the rules. Do you think AI would change the paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might, for the inspectors. They'd have more ways to check on us. That's the only thing I'd worry about here.

S0.say: It's mostly salesmen and city talk, like I've said all along. Farming is work, and work doesn't come out of a computer.
S0.think: My life stays as it is and I'm glad of it. My worries are the milk price, the bank and the rules, same as my father's, and AI was never going to milk my cows.
S0.do: Carries on exactly as he is, paying the mortgage and putting about 120 a month aside. Might replace the old bulk milk tank for about 15,000 if the milk price holds.
S0.feel: Calm and quietly satisfied he didn't fall for the hype.
S0.quote: I'd tell him a robot doesn't know when a cow's got mastitis just by the way she stands.
S0.fieldNote: Karl defines himself through four generations on the same farm. He sees AI as city talk and is more worried about inspectors and rules. His son is curious about robot milkers, which sets up a tension through the interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That's more likely, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms like mine have survived every change for a hundred years and we'll survive this one. I'd say it at the dairy meeting and mean it. People who work hard find a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry about the big dairies. If they get robot milkers and robot feeders, their costs drop and the milk price drops with it. A small family farm can't follow that without going into debt, and I won't borrow more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and work harder to keep costs down. We'd stop the holiday, put the 120 a month up to 200 and skip the new milk tank. I wouldn't buy a robot, not in the first year anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like weather coming in from the west.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Johann wants a robot milker. Would you listen to him now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd listen. I'm not sure I'd agree. A robot milker is 150,000, and I'm still paying for my sister's share. Maybe when he's older and it's his farm, he can make that choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the big dairies pushed you out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the robots, they're just machines. The government, for letting the big dairies get away with anything, and the supermarkets, for squeezing us. A fair market would give a family farm a chance.

S1.say: Farms like mine have survived every change for a hundred years, and we'll survive this one. People who work hard find a way.
S1.think: If the big dairies get robot milkers and feeders, their costs and the milk price drop. A small family farm can't follow that without going into debt, and I won't borrow more.
S1.do: Keeps going as he is and cuts costs harder, cancelling the holiday and the new milk tank. Raises savings from 120 to 200 a month and refuses to buy a robot in the first year.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like weather coming in from the west.
S1.quote: A fair market would give a family farm a chance.
S1.fieldNote: Karl publicly insists hard work will be enough, but privately fears big robot dairies driving down the price. He blames government and supermarkets, not the machines. He defers the robot decision to his son's generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not even one new herd of heifers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when a few big companies decide everything and nobody stops them. I'd say it at church, at the dairy meeting, everywhere. It's not right that a family farm can be wiped out in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the milk price falls through the floor and the bank starts phoning. I own the land, which is something, but the mortgage on my sister's share is still there. I'd be the Bauer who lost Lindenhof, and I can't stand to think it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First we'd cut everything: no holiday, Greta's car goes, Lotte's riding lessons stop. I'd talk to the bank early, before they talk to me, about stretching the mortgage. I'd lean on family too, my brother-in-law has a building firm and might need help in the winter. I'd go to our pastor as well, because I'd need someone to talk to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not be sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about buying a robot milker to keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years? No. I'd be borrowing 150,000 against a farm that's losing money. That's how you lose it faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Johann?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight, the farm might not be his. That would be the hardest thing I've ever said. My father never had to say it to me.

S2.say: This is what happens when a few big companies decide everything and nobody stops them. It's not right that a family farm can be wiped out in two years.
S2.think: The milk price falls through the floor and the bank starts phoning. I own the land, but the mortgage on my sister's share is still there, and I'd be the Bauer who lost Lindenhof.
S2.do: Cuts everything, including the holiday, Greta's car and Lotte's riding lessons. Talks to the bank early about stretching the mortgage and leans on family and his pastor, taking winter work with his brother-in-law's building firm if needed.
S2.quote: I'd tell him straight, the farm might not be his. That would be the hardest thing I've ever said.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI threatens Karl's sense of himself as a link in a family chain. He'd turn to family, church and the bank rather than government. He rejects buying robots as borrowing against a losing farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers need to stick together and keep the family farm alive. I'd also say the government should get out of the way and let us farm. Less paperwork would help more than any grant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd hold on for a few years, then it gets very hard. Five years is about when Johann finishes school. If he wanted to take it on with robots, that might be the way. If he didn't, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd save as much as we can, maybe 250 a month by cutting the holiday and the second car. I'd talk to Johann about an apprenticeship with the dairy machinery dealer, so he learns the machines properly. I'd keep milking the way I do, because that's what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The time helps, but it doesn't change much for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years you'd tell Johann the farm might not be his. What does five change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means he might be the one who saves it. He'd be twenty. He could learn the robots, and I'd still be there to teach him the cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd want Johann to learn the robots, but you won't touch them yourself. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. But I'm 43 and set in my ways, and he's fifteen. Every generation of Bauers did things a bit differently from the one before.

S3.say: Farmers need to stick together and keep the family farm alive. The government should get out of the way, because less paperwork would help more than any grant.
S3.think: I'd hold on for a few years, then it gets very hard. Five years is when Johann finishes school, and if he wanted to take it on with robots that might be the way.
S3.do: Saves about 250 a month by dropping the holiday and second car. Talks to Johann about an apprenticeship with the dairy machinery dealer and keeps milking the way he always has.
S3.feel: Anxious; the time helps but changes little for him personally.
S3.quote: He could learn the robots, and I'd still be there to teach him the cows.
S3.fieldNote: Karl's answer to five years is to pass the change on to his son through an apprenticeship. He accepts the contradiction of not learning the machines himself. He favours less regulation over public money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 53, Johann 25.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for the family farm to prepare, if the government doesn't strangle it with rules first. Families and churches will look after their own. I'd say that at the dairy meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be anxious for Johann, not me. I could probably keep farming the old way for ten years. But I'd be handing him a farm that can't compete unless he changes everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first years I'd do nothing different on the farm, just keep milking and saving, about 150 a month. I'd push Johann to do the machinery apprenticeship and maybe an agricultural course after. And I'd talk to Lotte about something away from farming, maybe nursing or teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more of a slow worry than a fright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any of the new machines, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe once Johann's running things. I'd let him put a robot feeder in and see how it goes. But I'd still be in the parlour at five in the morning, I'm sure of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Lindenhof to look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still Bauers on it, still cows on it. If there's robots too, so be it, as long as it's still a family farm and not owned by a company in the city.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time for the family farm to prepare, if the government doesn't strangle it with rules first. Families and churches will look after their own.
S4.think: I'm anxious for Johann, not me. I could keep farming the old way for ten years, but I'd be handing him a farm that can't compete unless he changes everything.
S4.do: Keeps milking and saving about 150 a month without changing the farm. Pushes Johann towards the machinery apprenticeship and an agricultural course, and talks to Lotte about a career away from farming.
S4.feel: Anxious, as a slow worry rather than a fright.
S4.quote: Still Bauers on it, still cows on it.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Karl's worry moves entirely to the handover to his son. He'd accept robots on the farm only if it stays in the family. He still sees himself in the parlour at five in the morning whatever happens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is no time at all for a farm, and I'd be the one who lost Lindenhof. What would help is a fair milk price and the government getting off our backs, so families have the room to sort themselves out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. When things go wrong, I go to church and talk to our pastor and the other farmers there. That's where I'd find my way through, not on a phone.

headlineQuote: When things go wrong, I go to church and talk to our pastor and the other farmers there.
portrait: Karl Bauer, 43, is the fourth generation to farm Lindenhof, an 80-cow family dairy, and carries a mortgage from buying out his sister's share. He never uses AI, dismisses it as city talk and blames government rules and supermarkets more than machines. He's calm if AI stalls, uneasy about big robot dairies under steady change and alarmed by fast AGI, which he fears would make him the Bauer who lost the farm. With more time he pins his hopes on his son learning the robots through an apprenticeship.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years is no time for a farm and he'd lose Lindenhof.
whatWouldHelp: A fair milk price and less government regulation, so families have room to sort things out themselves.
